title: Saim Chishti leaves for Hajj
titleOriginal: جناب صائم چشتی دی حج روانگی
takeaway: Lucky are the ones who get to stand at the Prophet's door. Send your greetings with them.
scene: The poet's friend, the poet and scholar Saim Chishti, is setting out on Hajj, the pilgrimage to Makkah and Madinah. The poet celebrates his good fortune and asks him to carry a message.

original: شمع رشد و ہدایت ول جا رہے نیں جاگے بھاگ نیں اج پروانیاں دے
جتھے سدا ملائک نیں جھکے رہندے لے کے بند رانیاں دے
transliteration: Shamaa-e-rushd-o-hidaayat val ja rahe nain, jaage bhaag nain ajj parwaaniyaan de
Jitthe sada malaa'ik nain jhuke rehnde, lai ke nazraane...
translation: They are heading toward the candle of right guidance; today the moths' luck has woken up.
There, where the angels are always bowing, bringing their offerings.
couplets.story: His friend is going toward the 'candle of guidance', the Prophet. The poet calls the pilgrims moths flying to that light, and says their luck has finally woken up. Where they're going, even the angels bow in respect.

original: ساقی کوثر نے بھر بھر جام دیندے کھلے در نیں اوتھے میخانیاں دے
نبی سوہنے توں پیئیں گا جام صائمؔ بخت جاگن گے احمدؔ نمانیاں دے
transliteration: Saaqi-e-Kausar ne bhar bhar jaam dende, khule dar nain othe maikhaaniyaan de
Nabi sohne ton peeyeen ga jaam Saim, bakht jaagan ge Ahmad nimaaniyaan de
translation: There the Saqi of Kausar pours cup after cup; the doors of the tavern stand open there.
Saim, you'll drink a cup from the beautiful Prophet's hand; Ahmad, the luck of the humble will awaken.
couplets.story: In Madinah, the Prophet, called the 'Saqi of Kausar', the one who pours from the river of paradise, generously gives out blessings, cup after cup. The doors are wide open. Saim will receive blessings straight from the Prophet, and even humble people will be lucky.

original: بختاں والیں سوہنیا مان موجاں اج چلیا ایں در حبیب ﷺ اتے
نظر کرم دی کر کریم دتی صائمؔ سخن ور شاعر ادیب اتے
transliteration: Bakhtaan vaaleen sohniya maan maujaan, ajj chaliya ain dar-e-Habib utte
Nazar karam di kar Kareem ditti Saim sukhan-var shaair adeeb utte
translation: Lucky one, enjoy it: today you are setting out for the door of the Beloved ﷺ.
The Generous One has turned His kind glance on Saim, the poet and man of letters.
couplets.story: He tells his friend to enjoy this blessed moment. He's on his way to the door of the Prophet, the 'Beloved' of God. God, the Generous, has looked kindly on Saim the poet.

original: دیکھ کویں پئے سارے نے رشک کردے تک سوہنیا تیرے نصیب اتے
جا کے روضے تے میرا اسلام آکھیں کرم کرنا اوہ احمدؔ غریب اتے
transliteration: Dekh kiven pae saare ne rashk karde, tak sohniya tere naseeb utte
Ja ke rauze te mera salaam aakheen, karam karna oh Ahmad gareeb utte
translation: Look how everyone is envious, my dear, of your good fortune.
When you reach the blessed tomb, give my greetings, and ask for kindness on poor Ahmad.
couplets.story: Everyone is a little jealous of how lucky he is. Then the poet's request: when you get to the Prophet's resting place in Madinah, please send my 'salaam', my greetings, and ask for blessings for poor Ahmad.

deeper:
This is one of the most openly devotional poems in the book. It is full of love for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: the 'candle of guidance', the 'Saqi of Kausar' and the 'Beloved' (Habib). Here the Sufi image of the saqi and the tavern is used for the Prophet's generosity in Madinah.

Asking a pilgrim to 'give my salaam at the rauza' is a cherished practice among Muslims who cannot make the journey themselves. Calling himself 'poor Ahmad' (Ahmad gareeb) is the humility of someone who longs to go but must stay behind.
why: It shows the warmth of devotion to the Prophet among the poet's friends, and the custom of sending greetings with pilgrims.
prompt: If a friend were going somewhere special to you, what message would you ask them to carry?
notes: Couplet 1, line 2: the end of the line is partly unclear ('بند رانیاں'), possibly 'nazraaniyaan' (offerings).
